title: The Most Misquoted Man in Europe
author: Friedrich Nietzsche
wiifm: Nietzsche is quoted on gym walls and was claimed by the Nazis, and almost everything people think he said is wrong. We follow a pastor's son who became a professor at twenty-four, lost his health, wandered Europe writing books nobody bought, and collapsed in Turin at forty-four, then watch his sister rebuild him into something he despised. You will come away with his real ideas, from where our values come from to the test of living your life again, and a sharp lesson in checking who edited what you are reading.

b: Friedrich Wilhelm Nietzsche was born on 15 October 1844 in the village of Röcken, in Prussian Saxony, on the birthday of the Prussian king he was named after. His father, Carl Ludwig, was the village's Lutheran pastor, and both his grandfathers had been churchmen too. Few philosophers have been born so deep inside the faith they would later take apart.

In 1849, when Friedrich was four, his father died after a brain illness. Months later his baby brother died too. The family moved to Naumburg, and the boy grew up in a house of women: his mother, his grandmother, two aunts and his younger sister, Elisabeth. Hold on to her. She will matter more than anyone in this story.

He was a solemn, devout, bookish child. Schoolfellows are said to have called him the little pastor, because he could recite Bible passages and hymns so movingly that listeners were close to tears. At fourteen he won a place at Schulpforta, the most demanding boarding school in Germany, where he was drilled in Greek and Latin from dawn to dusk.

At university, first in Bonn and then Leipzig, he dropped the theology his family expected, and his faith went with it. He found two things instead. One was the study of classical texts, under the great scholar Friedrich Ritschl. The other was a second-hand copy of Schopenhauer's The World as Will and Representation, picked up in a Leipzig bookshop in 1865, which hit him like a revelation.
ch.cap: The 'little pastor' recites scripture and listeners weep

b: Ritschl thought him the most gifted student he had ever taught, and said so in writing. On that recommendation, in 1869, the University of Basel in Switzerland made Nietzsche professor of classical philology at twenty-four, before he had finished his doctorate. Leipzig hurriedly awarded him one without an examination. He was a prodigy by any measure.

In Switzerland he grew close to Richard Wagner, who was living at Tribschen near Lucerne, and to his partner, later his wife, Cosima. For a few years the young professor was almost a member of the household, convinced that Wagner's music could revive the tragic spirit of ancient Greece. His first book, The Birth of Tragedy, published in 1872, argued exactly that, and it so annoyed his fellow scholars that it damaged his academic standing.

In 1870, during the Franco-Prussian War, he volunteered as a medical orderly. He caught dysentery and diphtheria, and he was never really well again. From then on his life was a cycle of crushing migraines, vomiting, insomnia and failing eyesight, sometimes days at a time in a darkened room.

The friendship with Wagner did not last. Nietzsche came to see the composer's turn towards Christian piety and German nationalism, and the antisemitism of his circle, as everything he distrusted. By 1878, when he published Human, All Too Human, the break was complete. It was the first of several breaks with people who wanted to use him for their own causes, and the pattern is worth noticing.
ch.cap: Young Professor Nietzsche listens to Wagner at Tribschen

b: In 1879, at thirty-four, Nietzsche resigned his chair because of illness, and Basel gave him a small pension. He had given up his Prussian citizenship when he moved to Switzerland, and for the next ten years he lived as a stateless, wandering invalid, moving with the seasons between cheap rented rooms: summers in the mountain village of Sils-Maria in Switzerland, winters in Genoa, Nice and later Turin, chasing the air and light that eased his head.

He wrote constantly, often while walking for hours, and he wrote in aphorisms and short numbered sections, partly because that was what his eyes and headaches allowed. The form had consequences. He argues in flashes rather than chains, so almost any position can be supported by a genuine quotation from him.

In 1882 he fell for a brilliant young Russian woman, Lou Salomé, and proposed, and she turned him down. His sister Elisabeth, jealous, worked hard to drive her away. The episode left him lonelier than ever, and in a burst of creation over the next few years he wrote Thus Spoke Zarathustra.

Almost nobody bought any of it. When he finished the fourth and final part of Zarathustra he could not find a publisher, so he had about forty copies printed at his own expense and gave away only a handful. The most quoted philosopher of the twentieth century spent the 1880s writing for a few friends.
ch.cap: The wandering invalid writes aphorisms as he walks
ch.when: Sils-Maria, Genoa, Nice and Turin, 1879 to 1888

b: His most famous sentence comes from The Gay Science, published in 1882, and it is almost always heard backwards. In section 125 a madman lights a lantern in the bright morning, runs into the marketplace and cries out that he is looking for God. The people standing around are not believers. They are unbelievers, and they laugh at him. Has God got lost, they jeer. Has he emigrated?

So the madman turns on them. God is dead, he says, and we have killed him, you and I. Then come the questions that are the real substance. What were we doing when we unchained this earth from its sun? Where is it moving now? Is there still an up or a down? How shall we comfort ourselves, the murderers of all murderers? The crowd falls silent. The madman throws down his lantern and says he has come too early. The news has not yet reached people's ears.

This is not a victory speech. It is the report of a catastrophe, delivered to comfortable people who have not understood what their own unbelief implies. European morality, Nietzsche thought, was a cathedral built on a foundation that had now been removed, and most people were still living in the building without noticing. The danger he named was nihilism: the state in which the old values have lost their authority and nothing has replaced them, so nothing seems worth doing.

And here is what makes him, read properly, a builder rather than a wrecker. If values are human creations, they can be created deliberately and well. His late project was what he called a revaluation of all values. The question he leaves you with is not whether God exists. It is which values you will live by, knowing that you chose them.
ch.cap: A madman with a lantern searches the market for God

b: In August 1881, walking beside the lake of Silvaplana near Sils-Maria, Nietzsche stopped by a huge pyramid-shaped rock, and an idea came to him that he later described as six thousand feet beyond man and time. He called it eternal recurrence, and in The Gay Science he called it the heaviest weight.

Imagine, he writes, that a demon crept after you into your loneliest loneliness and told you that you must live this life again, and innumerable times more, with nothing new in it, every pain and joy and every small thing in the same order. Would you throw yourself down, gnash your teeth and curse the demon? Or have you ever had a moment when you would answer: you are a god, and I have never heard anything more divine?

It works whether or not the cosmology is true, and that is the point. It tests whether you can say yes to your actual life, with its compromises, rather than to an imagined better one. From it comes his formula for greatness, amor fati, love of fate. That is not Stoic acceptance. It is something stranger and harder: wanting what happened.

Its shadow is the figure he feared most. In the prologue to Zarathustra he sketches the last man, and he is not a monster. He is comfortable. A little pleasure for the day, a little for the night, nothing strenuous, no great love and no great contempt. We have invented happiness, say the last men, and they blink. When Zarathustra offers the crowd something higher, they shout back: give us the last man. Set that beside the Stoics. A life arranged entirely around not being disturbed may end up very small.

As a business exercise it makes a sharp annual review. If you had to live this exact year again, endlessly, with these clients, this schedule and these difficult relationships, would you say yes? Mark what you would refuse. That is what to change.
ch.cap: Beside the pyramid rock, the heaviest thought strikes

ch.h: Where good and evil came from
b: In 1887 he published On the Genealogy of Morality, and its method is what makes him dangerous. Where other philosophers ask whether a moral claim is true, Nietzsche asks where it came from, who made it and what it did for them.

His story runs like this. In the ancient world, he claims, good belonged to the strong, the healthy and the well-born. It meant noble, and its opposite was not evil but bad, in the sense of low and contemptible. This is master morality, a frank self-affirmation. Then came an inversion, led by priests. A subjugated people who could not defeat the strong did something cleverer: they reinterpreted. Weakness became meekness, and meekness became a virtue. Being unable to strike back became forgiveness. And strength, health and appetite were renamed evil.

The engine of this, he says, is ressentiment, a French word he uses because the German for resentment is too thin. It is a long-stored grudge that, unable to act, turns creative and invents values. The slave revolt in morality, he writes, begins when ressentiment itself becomes creative and gives birth to values.

Three qualifications stop this sliding into caricature. Nietzsche thought the revolt succeeded and made humans far deeper and more interesting, giving us conscience and an inner life. The book is a diagnosis, not an instruction to be cruel. And master and slave are ways of valuing, found in almost everyone, not classes of people. What it gives you is a permanent question: whose interests does this moral consensus serve, and who built it? Try it on your own industry's accepted best practice. Some rule everybody obeys was probably invented because it suited the big players.

Two more terms need rescuing. Will to power is not the urge to dominate others, which he often treats as a sign of weakness. It is the drive of living things to grow, overcome resistance and express their strength, in an artist finishing hard work as much as in a conqueror. And the Übermensch, the overman, is not a race or a political programme. He is someone who, with no God to hand down values, creates his own and lives by them without resentment. Nietzsche's examples were Goethe and, with reservations, Napoleon. Alongside both runs perspectivism: there is no view from nowhere, so look through as many eyes as you can.
ch.cap: Priests tip the nobles' 'good' over into 'evil'

b: In 1885 Elisabeth married Bernhard Förster, a former schoolteacher and one of the loudest antisemitic agitators in Germany. Nietzsche stayed away from the wedding. He made his disgust plain to her, and in a draft letter around Christmas 1887 he told her that her tie to an antisemitic leader was a constant source of ill humour and gloom to him.

In 1886 the couple sailed to Paraguay with a small band of settlers to found a colony of racially pure Germans, which they called Nueva Germania. It was a disaster of poor land, disease, debt and angry colonists. In June 1889 Förster, facing ruin and exposure, killed himself in a hotel room.

Meanwhile Nietzsche made his views clear to anyone who would listen. In 1887 he wrote to the antisemitic publisher Theodor Fritsch, who kept sending him his journal, demanding that it stop. He mocked German nationalism constantly, and called himself a good European.
Remember all of this, because within a few years almost none of it would be easy to find in print. Elisabeth was coming home.
ch.cap: Elisabeth and Förster found Nueva Germania in Paraguay

b: In 1888 Nietzsche was living in Turin and writing at a furious pace: Twilight of the Idols, The Antichrist, The Case of Wagner, and the strange autobiography Ecce Homo, with chapters titled Why I Am So Wise and Why I Write Such Good Books. His letters grew euphoric. Something was going badly wrong.

In the first days of January 1889 he collapsed in the street. Then came the so-called madness letters, short notes signed Dionysus or The Crucified, sent to friends and public figures. In one, he declared that he was having all antisemites shot. His friend Franz Overbeck hurried from Basel and brought him back to a clinic.

Everyone knows the story that goes with this: Nietzsche sees a cab driver beating a horse, throws his arms around its neck in tears, and collapses. It is irresistible, the philosopher of hardness undone by pity. But the evidence is thin. The horse appears only in later reports, the earliest apparently a newspaper account from 1900, more than eleven years on, drawing on what his landlord's household remembered. The tears and the embrace grew with each retelling. Something happened in the street. The horse may be legend.

He never recovered. The cause is still argued over: the old diagnosis was syphilis, but some doctors now suggest a slow-growing brain tumour or an inherited disorder. He lived eleven more years, silent and dependent, cared for first by his mother in Naumburg and, after her death in 1897, by Elisabeth in Weimar. He died there on 25 August 1900, just as his fame was exploding.
ch.cap: In a Turin street, Nietzsche collapses beside a cab horse

b: Elisabeth came back from Paraguay to find her brother helpless and his papers unguarded. She took control of everything. In 1894 she founded the Nietzsche Archive, later moving it to Weimar, decided who could see the manuscripts, and set about managing his reputation. She even showed her invalid brother to visitors, dressed in a white robe.

With the composer Heinrich Köselitz, whom Nietzsche had nicknamed Peter Gast, she took the huge mass of unpublished notebooks and assembled a book called The Will to Power, presented as the systematic masterpiece her brother had been building towards. The first edition in 1901 had four hundred and eighty-three sections. The second, in 1906, had one thousand and sixty-seven. That version shaped his reputation for half a century.

But Nietzsche had abandoned that plan. The title first appears in his notes in 1885, and in late August 1888 he replaced it with Attempt at a Revaluation of All Values, then put some of the material into Twilight of the Idols and The Antichrist. In the 1960s two Italian scholars, Giorgio Colli and Mazzino Montinari, worked through the original manuscripts to produce a proper critical edition. Their verdict on The Will to Power was blunt: a historical forgery, with its order imposed and fragments cut and stitched together without telling the reader.

By then the damage was done. Elisabeth embraced the Nazi movement. Hitler visited the archive, and she gave him her brother's walking stick. When she died in 1935, he came to her funeral. The man who stayed away from her wedding, broke with Wagner's circle and, in the wreckage of his mind, called for antisemites to be shot became, through his sister's hands, a prophet of the Third Reich.

The rescue in English came largely from Walter Kaufmann, whose 1950 study and translations presented a Nietzsche who was anti-nationalist and opposed to antisemitism. Kaufmann probably over-corrected, smoothing away some genuinely harsh edges, but he was arguing against half a century of falsification, and he won.
ch.cap: Elisabeth stitches her brother's notes into a fake book

ch.h: What is actually wrong with him
b: A fair primer has to cut both ways, because some real objections survive the rescue.

His writing on women is bad. Not misread, not a matter of context: a string of contemptuous aphorisms that even his most sympathetic readers can only note, not defend. His contempt for equality is genuine too. He despised democracy and socialism, saw equality as ressentiment in political clothes, and was pleased when the Danish critic Georg Brandes called his position aristocratic radicalism. You can use the genealogical method without that politics, but you should not pretend it is not in the text.

And the line everybody knows, what does not kill me makes me stronger, from the opening maxims of Twilight of the Idols, is an aphorism from a chronically ill man having a good day, not a finding. The research on trauma is clear that adversity often does not strengthen people. It damages them. Quote it as rhetoric. Never offer it as advice to someone who is actually suffering.

What remains is still a great deal. Ask where any value came from and whose interests it served. Treat nihilism as a real problem, and answer it by choosing your values on purpose. Put your life to the test of living it again. Watch for the comfortable last man in yourself. Look through as many eyes as you can.

And carry the lesson of his afterlife into everything you read. Before you trust anyone's final masterpiece, a founder's last letter, a posthumous memoir, a will, ask who held the manuscripts, and what they wanted.
ch.cap: A reader weighs Nietzsche, magnifier over his notebooks

take: Ask where a value came from
For any rule presented as obviously right, ask who introduced it, when, and whose situation it suited. It is corrosive, sometimes unfair, and indispensable.

Take three unquestioned norms in your sector, such as standard margins or payment terms, and find the player each one originally helped. One is usually a big competitor's cost structure dressed as a moral rule.

A stored grudge that cannot act will invent values instead, renaming what it cannot do as virtue. Watch for moral language in yourself or a team that happens to flatter exactly what its speakers cannot do.
God is dead is a warning
The madman is laughed at by unbelievers, and his point is the danger of nihilism once old foundations go. Values you know you made can still be chosen deliberately and well.
Submit the year to eternal recurrence
Would you live this exact year again, endlessly, with these clients and this schedule? Mark what you would refuse; that is what to change.
A life built entirely around comfort and not being disturbed shrinks. Set Nietzsche's warning against the Stoic wish for calm and keep the tension.
Write your strongest belief about your business, then build the two best cases against it. If you cannot, you have held the view a long time rather than understood it.
Check who edited what you read
The Will to Power was assembled by his sister from abandoned notes and later called a forgery. Before citing any posthumous work, ask who held the papers and what they wanted.
recall: Summarise the First Essay of the Genealogy and the three qualifications that block the caricature.

Good once meant noble and strong, with bad meaning low; a priestly revolt driven by ressentiment renamed weakness as virtue and strength as evil. But Nietzsche thought the revolt made humanity deeper, he was diagnosing rather than prescribing, and master and slave are ways of valuing present in almost everyone, not classes of people.
Who says God is dead, to whom, and what is the passage really about?

A madman with a lantern, in a morning marketplace, to unbelievers who laugh at him. The substance is his questions about unchaining the earth from its sun; it is a warning about nihilism, not an atheist boast, and he concludes he has come too early.
What is the test of eternal recurrence, and how does amor fati differ from Stoic acceptance?

A demon says you must live this exact life endlessly; do you curse him, or call it divine? Amor fati, love of fate, asks you to actively want what happened, which is stronger than the Stoic acceptance of what cannot be changed.
What is wrong with reading will to power and the Übermensch as calls for domination?

Nietzsche often treats crude domination as weakness; will to power is the drive to grow and overcome resistance, seen in artists and ascetics too. The overman is a self-creator who makes and lives by his own values, with Goethe as an example, not a race or political programme.
How was The Will to Power made, and what did scholars conclude?

Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche and Heinrich Köselitz assembled it from his notebooks, with 483 sections in 1901 and 1,067 in 1906, though he had dropped the plan in August 1888. Colli and Montinari, working from the manuscripts in the 1960s, called it a historical forgery.
note: Life dates, the Basel appointment, the 1888 change of plan and the Colli and Montinari critical edition are well documented, as are his letters against antisemitism and the madness notes of January 1889. The Turin horse story rests on late, second-hand reports and is probably embellished or legendary; the cause of his illness remains disputed. Hitler's visits to the archive and the gift of the walking stick are widely reported in biographies such as Sue Prideaux's I Am Dynamite!, 2018. Kaufmann's rehabilitation is now thought to have softened Nietzsche's genuinely anti-egalitarian views.
words: The scholarly study of languages and texts, especially ancient ones, and how they were written and transmitted.
Nietzsche became professor of classical philology at Basel at twenty-four, and it was philology again, by Colli and Montinari, that exposed his sister's version of The Will to Power.
The belief that nothing has real value or meaning, so nothing is worth doing.
Nietzsche did not preach nihilism; he warned that it would follow the death of God unless people deliberately created new values to live by.
A long-stored, powerless grudge that turns creative and reshapes values to condemn whoever is resented.
In On the Genealogy of Morality, Nietzsche makes ressentiment the engine that turned weakness into meekness and meekness into a virtue.
Written in short, pithy sayings rather than continuous argument.
Partly because of his failing eyes and migraines, Nietzsche wrote in aphoristic flashes, which is why almost any view can be backed with a genuine quotation from him.
An idealised, uncritical biography that treats its subject as a saint.
Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche turned the Nietzsche Archive into a hagiography factory, displaying her invalid brother in a white robe and shaping his legacy to suit her politics.
stories: Everyone knows Nietzsche said God is dead. Almost nobody knows the scene. A madman lights a lantern in the bright morning and runs into the marketplace crying that he is looking for God. The crowd are not believers. They are unbelievers, and they laugh: has God got lost, has he emigrated? So he turns on them. God is dead, and we have killed him, you and I. What did we do when we unchained the earth from its sun? The crowd falls silent. He throws down his lantern and says he has come too early. It is not a victory cry. It is a warning to comfortable people.

Nietzsche loathed antisemitism. He stayed away from his sister Elisabeth's wedding to a notorious antisemitic agitator, and demanded that an antisemitic publisher stop sending him his journal. Then he collapsed, and for his last eleven years Elisabeth controlled him and his papers. She founded an archive, displayed her helpless brother to visitors in a white robe, and stitched his abandoned notes into a masterpiece he never wrote, The Will to Power, later called a historical forgery by the scholars who checked the manuscripts. She embraced the Nazis. Hitler visited, and she gave him her brother's walking stick. When she died in 1935, he came to her funeral.

The story goes like this. In January 1889, on a street in Turin, Nietzsche sees a cab driver beating a horse, throws his arms around its neck in tears, and collapses, never to recover his mind. It is irresistible: the philosopher of hardness undone by pity. The trouble is the evidence. The horse appears only in later reports, the earliest apparently a newspaper account from 1900, more than eleven years on, and the tears and the embrace grew with each retelling. He certainly collapsed that January and began sending letters signed Dionysus. The horse may be legend. It is a good test of how much we want a story to be true.
biz: Ask who invented the best practice

Nietzsche asked where a value came from and whose interests it served. Apply that to lead-generation norms: call within a minute, call ten times, chase on WhatsApp until they answer, show the lowest representative rate in the headline. Some of this helps customers, some was invented because it suited high-volume sellers. For each practice, ask who benefits and test it against Consumer Duty. Then measure, rather than assume: compare contact cadences against opt-outs, complaints and completed cases, not just connection rate. Keep what serves the customer and the business together, and drop what only serves the dashboard.

Elisabeth's lesson is to ask who edited what you are reading. Most numbers you receive have an editor: ad platforms report conversions on their own attribution, lead suppliers report their own quality, agencies summarise their own results. Once a month, reconcile platform-reported conversions for each channel against your own CRM and Case Review Tracker, counting only enquiries that reached a real conversation and then a lender submission. Note the gap per channel and how it moves. Budget suggestions to Grok should rest on your reconciled figures, not on the most flattering version of events.
connects: Nietzsche's claim that values are human creations rather than discoveries anticipates Harari's argument that shared fictions such as gods, nations and money hold societies together.
Both Nietzsche and Haidt ask where moral feelings come from and whose purposes they serve, rather than simply whether moral claims are true.
Machiavelli and Nietzsche both scandalised readers by separating power from Christian morality, and both were then caricatured by people who never read them closely.
recap:
Friedrich Nietzsche was born in eighteen forty-four, in a Prussian village, the son of a Lutheran pastor. His father died when he was four, and he grew up in a house of women, including a younger sister called Elisabeth, who would matter more than anyone in his story. He was such a devout child that schoolfellows called him the little pastor. At university he lost his faith and found two things instead: ancient texts, and the gloomy philosopher Schopenhauer.

He was a prodigy. At twenty-four he became a professor in Basel before he had even finished his doctorate. He fell in with Richard Wagner, then broke with him over Wagner's nationalism and the antisemitism of his circle. Illness from his time as a wartime medical orderly wrecked his health, and at thirty-four he resigned. For ten years he wandered between cheap rooms in Switzerland and Italy, writing in short flashes because his eyes and headaches allowed nothing longer. Almost nobody bought his books.

Here are the ideas, the real ones. First, God is dead, and it is not a boast. It is a warning that the foundations of European morality had gone, and that nihilism, the sense that nothing is worth doing, would follow unless we chose new values on purpose.

Second, the heaviest weight. Imagine living this exact life again, endlessly. Would you curse that, or welcome it? From this comes love of fate, wanting what actually happened.

Third, beware the last man, comfortable and small, who has invented happiness and blinks.

Fourth, genealogy. Ask not only whether a value is true, but where it came from and whose interests it served.

In January eighteen eighty-nine he collapsed in Turin and never recovered. The famous story of him embracing a beaten horse may well be legend. Elisabeth, back from a failed colony in Paraguay, took control of him and his papers. She stitched his notes into a book he had abandoned, The Will to Power, and gave his walking stick to Hitler. The man who called for antisemites to be shot became, through her hands, a prophet of the Nazis. Later scholars rescued him.

He is not clean. His writing on women is contemptuous, he despised equality, and what does not kill me makes me stronger is rhetoric, not advice for anyone suffering.

The line to remember: before you trust anyone's final masterpiece, ask who held the manuscripts, and what they wanted.
